topic.title: Sorting Algorithms
topic.summary: Bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick and counting sort — how they work, their complexity and stability, and which sort to use when (including what Python, Java and JavaScript use internally).
topic.overview:
**Why sorting still shows up in interviews.** You will rarely write a sort at work, yet sorting questions test loops, recursion, invariants and complexity analysis in one go — and many problems become easy once the data is sorted (two pointers, merging intervals, finding duplicates). Service companies and banks often ask you to write bubble, selection or insertion sort on paper; product companies ask merge sort, quicksort partitioning and "which sort would you use, and why?".

**What you must be able to do**
- Write **bubble, selection and insertion sort** from memory and state their best/worst cases.
- Write **merge sort** and explain T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n), O(n) extra space, stable.
- Write **quicksort with Lomuto partition**, explain the worst case (sorted input with a fixed pivot) and how a random pivot fixes it.
- Explain **stability** with an example, and **counting sort** for small integer ranges.
- Know what the **built-in sorts** use: TimSort (Python, Java objects, V8) and dual-pivot quicksort (Java primitives).

**How to study it**
1. Implement each algorithm once without looking, then trace it by hand on 5–6 numbers.
2. For each, say one sentence of *why* it has its complexity (not just the Big-O).
3. Memorise the comparison table (best/average/worst, space, stable, in-place).
4. Practise the "sort first" trick on problems like meeting rooms, 3Sum and merging intervals.

cheatsheet.title: Complexities
points: Bubble / selection / insertion: O(n²) average; bubble and insertion are O(n) on sorted input
Merge sort: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space
Quicksort: O(n log n) expected, O(n²) worst, O(log n) stack, in place
Heap sort: O(n log n) always, O(1) extra space, not stable
Counting sort: O(n + k) for integer keys in a range of size k
Any comparison sort: Ω(n log n) worst case

cheatsheet.title: Stability
points: Stable = equal keys keep their input order
Stable: bubble, insertion, merge, counting, TimSort
Multi-key trick: sort by the secondary key, then stable-sort by the primary key

cheatsheet.title: Built-in sorts
points: Java `Arrays.sort(int[])`: dual-pivot quicksort; objects and `List.sort`: TimSort, stable
JavaScript (V8): TimSort, stable since ES2019 — default compares as strings, pass `(a, b) => a - b`

cheatsheet.title: Things interviewers listen for
points: Insertion sort is O(n + inversions) — great for nearly sorted data
Quicksort worst case comes from bad pivots; randomise
Merge sort is the way to sort a linked list and data larger than RAM
In real code, call the library sort

patterns.name: Custom comparator
patterns.whenToUse: Sorting objects or by several keys; numbers in JavaScript (default sort is lexicographic).

template.code:
// ascending by price, then by name for ties
items.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));

patterns.name: Lomuto partition
patterns.whenToUse: Quicksort, quickselect (k-th smallest), splitting an array around a value.

patterns.name: Merge two sorted arrays
patterns.whenToUse: Merge sort, merging sorted lists/files, intersections and unions of sorted data.

patterns.whenToUse: Interval problems (meeting rooms, merge intervals), duplicates, pairs/triplets with two pointers.

questions.title: Bubble Sort
questions.prompt:
Implement **bubble sort**: sort an integer array in ascending order **in place** by repeatedly swapping adjacent elements that are out of order.

Then explain its best, average and worst case, and how to make it stop early on an already-sorted array.

examples.explanation: One pass with no swaps, then stop: O(n).
Equal values are never swapped, so the sort is stable.

constraints: 0 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10³ (it is O(n²), so not for big inputs)
hints: Compare `arr[j]` with `arr[j + 1]`. What happens to the largest value during one left-to-right sweep?
After pass k the last k elements are final — the inner loop can stop earlier each pass.
Track whether a pass swapped anything; if not, the array is sorted and you can break.

approaches.name: Plain bubble sort
approaches.idea: n − 1 full passes of neighbour comparisons, always.

approaches.name: Shrinking inner loop
approaches.idea: After pass p the last p elements are final, so compare only up to n − 1 − p.

approaches.name: Early exit with a swapped flag
approaches.idea: Stop as soon as a pass makes no swaps.

solution.summary: Make passes over the array, swapping neighbours that are out of order; each pass bubbles the largest remaining value to the end, so the inner loop shrinks by one each time. A `swapped` flag stops early when a pass makes no swaps. O(n²) worst/average, O(n) best, O(1) space, stable.
solution.explanation:
**How it works**
1. For `pass = 0 … n − 2`: walk `j` from 0 to `n − 2 − pass`.
2. If `arr[j] > arr[j + 1]`, swap them.
3. After the pass, the largest unsorted value is at index `n − 1 − pass` — it never moves again.
4. If a pass made no swap, every adjacent pair is ordered, so the array is sorted: `break`.

**Why it is correct.** Invariant: after pass p, the last p + 1 positions hold the p + 1 largest values in sorted order. A sweep always carries the current maximum to the right because it wins every comparison it takes part in.

**Complexity.** Worst case (reversed input) does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons and as many swaps → O(n²). Best case (already sorted) with the flag: one pass, n − 1 comparisons, 0 swaps → O(n). Memory O(1).

**Stability.** We swap only when `arr[j] > arr[j + 1]` (strictly), so equal values never pass each other: **stable**. Using `>=` would break that.

**When would anyone use it?** Almost never in production — insertion sort does the same job with fewer writes. It is asked because it shows you understand loops, invariants and complexity. Its one niche: detecting "is this already sorted / almost sorted?" in one cheap pass.

complexity.time: O(n²) average and worst (n(n − 1)/2 comparisons); O(n) best with the swapped flag

keyPoints: Each pass bubbles the largest remaining value to its final position
Inner loop bound shrinks: `j < n − 1 − pass`
The `swapped` flag gives an O(n) best case
Stable because equal neighbours are not swapped
O(1) extra space; too slow (O(n²)) for large inputs

visuals.title: Bubble sort on [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]
visuals.caption: Blue = the pair just swapped, orange = compared without swapping, green = final positions.

steps.note: Bubble sort repeatedly compares **neighbours** and swaps them when they are out of order. Each pass carries the largest remaining value to the end, like a bubble rising.
Pass 0, j = 0: compare 5 and 1. 5 > 1, so swap them.
Pass 0, j = 1: compare 5 and 4. 5 > 4, so swap them.
Pass 0, j = 2: compare 5 and 2. 5 > 2, so swap them.
Pass 0, j = 3: compare 5 and 8. 5 ≤ 8, already in order — no swap. End of pass 0: 8 is now in its final place.
Pass 1, j = 0: compare 1 and 4. 1 ≤ 4, already in order — no swap.
Pass 1, j = 1: compare 4 and 2. 4 > 2, so swap them.
Pass 1, j = 2: compare 4 and 5. 4 ≤ 5, already in order — no swap. End of pass 1: 5 is now in its final place.
Pass 2, j = 0: compare 1 and 2. 1 ≤ 2, already in order — no swap.
Pass 2, j = 1: compare 2 and 4. 2 ≤ 4, already in order — no swap. End of pass 2: 4 is now in its final place.
Pass 2 made **no swaps**, so every neighbour pair is in order and the whole array is sorted. `break` early — this check is what makes the best case O(n). Result: [1, 2, 4, 5, 8].

visuals.title: Measured work for n = 8 (with the early-exit flag)
visuals.caption: Counts come from running the solution above. Reversed input is the worst case: 28 = 8·7/2 comparisons and swaps.

pitfalls: Running the inner loop to `n − 1` every pass — still correct but wastes comparisons, or to `n` — reads past the end
Forgetting to reset `swapped = false` at the start of each pass
Using `>=` in the comparison, which makes the sort unstable
Claiming bubble sort is O(n) without the early-exit flag

followUps.question: Is bubble sort stable? In place?
followUps.answer: Both: it only swaps strictly greater neighbours (stable) and uses O(1) extra memory (in place).

followUps.question: How is it different from insertion sort?
followUps.answer: Both are O(n²) and stable, but insertion sort shifts each new element left into a sorted prefix, doing far fewer writes and running in O(n + inversions) — which is why real libraries use insertion sort (not bubble sort) for small or nearly sorted ranges.

questions.title: Selection Sort
questions.prompt:
Implement **selection sort** to sort an integer array in ascending order in place: repeatedly find the minimum of the unsorted part and move it to the end of the sorted part.

State its complexity and whether it is stable.
constraints: Sort in place with O(1) extra memory
hints: Which value belongs at index 0? Find it, then put it there.
Repeat for index 1 using only the remaining elements. How many comparisons does each round need?
Round i: scan `arr[i..n−1]` for `minIdx`, then swap `arr[i]` with `arr[minIdx]`. At most one swap per round.

approaches.name: Selection sort
approaches.idea: n − 1 rounds; each scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and swaps it into place.

approaches.name: Heap sort (the "fast selection sort")
approaches.idea: Keep the unsorted part in a heap so "find the min/max" costs O(log n) instead of O(n).

solution.summary: For each position i, scan the unsorted part for the minimum and swap it into position i. It always does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons (O(n²) even on sorted input) but at most n − 1 swaps, uses O(1) space, and is not stable.
solution.explanation:
**How it works**
1. For `i = 0 … n − 2`: set `minIdx = i`.
2. For `j = i + 1 … n − 1`: if `arr[j] < arr[minIdx]`, update `minIdx`.
3. Swap `arr[i]` and `arr[minIdx]` (skip if equal indices).

**Invariant.** After round i, `arr[0..i]` holds the i + 1 smallest values in sorted order and is never touched again.

**Complexity.** The scans cost (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons **regardless of the input** — selection sort cannot exploit sorted data, so best = average = worst = O(n²). It performs at most **n − 1 swaps**, the fewest of the simple sorts, which matters only when writes are very expensive (e.g. flash memory wear).

**Not stable.** The swap moves `arr[i]` far to the right, possibly jumping over an equal key (see the second visual). Not adaptive either.

**Relation to heap sort.** Heap sort is selection sort with a smarter "find the extreme" step (a heap), turning O(n²) into O(n log n).

complexity.time: O(n²) always — n(n − 1)/2 comparisons even if the input is sorted
complexity.space: O(1) — in place, at most n − 1 swaps

keyPoints: Select the minimum of the unsorted part, swap it to the front
Always O(n²) comparisons: not adaptive
At most n − 1 swaps: useful only when writes are expensive
Not stable: the long-distance swap can reorder equal keys
Heap sort is selection sort with a heap

visuals.title: Selection sort on [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]
visuals.caption: Light-blue range = unsorted part being scanned, orange = current minimum, green = final prefix.

steps.note: Selection sort grows a sorted prefix on the left. In round i it **selects** the minimum of the unsorted part `arr[i..n−1]` and swaps it into position i.
Round i = 0: scan indices 0…4 (4 comparisons). The smallest value is 10 at index 1.
Swap `arr[0]` (29) with `arr[1]` (10). Index 0 now holds its final value; only one swap per round.
Round i = 1: scan indices 1…4 (3 comparisons). The smallest value is 13 at index 4.
Swap `arr[1]` (29) with `arr[4]` (13). Index 1 now holds its final value; only one swap per round.
Round i = 2: scan indices 2…4 (2 comparisons). The smallest value is 14 at index 2.
The minimum is already at index 2 (`minIdx === i`), so no swap is needed.
Round i = 3: scan indices 3…4 (1 comparison). The smallest value is 29 at index 4.
Swap `arr[3]` (37) with `arr[4]` (29). Index 3 now holds its final value; only one swap per round.
After n − 1 rounds the last element is automatically the largest. Sorted: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37] with 10 comparisons (always) but only 3 swaps.

visuals.title: Why selection sort is not stable
visuals.caption: Light blue = 4a, orange = 4b (equal keys). Watch the swap in round 0.

steps.note: Two records have the same key 4: **4a** comes before **4b** in the input. A stable sort must keep 4a before 4b.
i = 0: the minimum 1 is at index 3; swapping it into index 0 throws **4a** to index 3 — right over 4b. The long-distance swap just reversed the order of the two equal keys.
i = 1: the minimum (2) is already in place.
i = 2: the minimum (4b) is already in place — `4a < 4b` is false (they are equal), so they are not swapped back.

Final order: 1, 2, **4b, 4a**. The keys are sorted, but equal keys changed their relative order — selection sort is **not stable**. (A stable variant would shift elements right instead of swapping, at the cost of more writes.)

pitfalls: Swapping inside the inner loop every time a smaller value is found (that is a slower variant of exchange sort, not selection sort)
Claiming an O(n) best case — selection sort always scans the full suffix
Saying it is stable
Inner loop starting at `i` instead of `i + 1` (harmless) or ending at `n − 1` (misses the last element)

followUps.question: When could selection sort be the right choice?
followUps.answer: Tiny arrays where code size matters, or when each write is far more expensive than a read, because it does at most n − 1 swaps. Otherwise insertion sort is better.

followUps.question: How can you make it stable?
followUps.answer: Instead of swapping, remove the minimum and shift the elements between i and minIdx one place right before inserting it at i. That keeps equal keys in order but costs O(n) writes per round.

questions.title: Insertion Sort
questions.prompt: Implement **insertion sort** to sort an integer array in ascending order in place. Explain why it is fast on nearly sorted input and why real-world library sorts still use it.

examples.explanation: Only one shift is needed — nearly sorted input is almost O(n).

constraints: 0 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10³ for arbitrary input (O(n²) worst case)
hints: Think of sorting a hand of cards: keep the left part sorted and add one card at a time.
To insert `key = arr[i]`, walk left while elements are bigger than `key`. Instead of swapping, what can you do with them?
Save `key`, shift every larger element one slot right, then write `key` into the gap at `j + 1`.

approaches.name: Swap-based insertion
approaches.idea: Swap the new element leftwards while it is smaller than its neighbour. Correct, but 3 writes per step.

approaches.name: Shift-based insertion
approaches.idea: Hold the key aside, shift larger elements right, write the key once.
approaches.time: O(n + inversions): O(n) best, O(n²) worst

approaches.name: Binary insertion sort
approaches.idea: Binary-search the insert position (O(log n) comparisons), but shifting is still O(n) per element. Used inside TimSort for short runs.
approaches.time: O(n log n) comparisons, O(n²) moves

solution.summary: Keep the left part sorted; for each new element, save it as `key`, shift the larger elements of the sorted part one slot right, and drop `key` into the gap. O(n²) worst case, O(n) on sorted input, O(1) space, stable — and fast on small or nearly sorted arrays, which is why TimSort uses it for short runs.
solution.explanation:
**How it works**
1. For `i = 1 … n − 1`: `key = arr[i]`, `j = i − 1`.
2. While `j ≥ 0` and `arr[j] > key`: `arr[j + 1] = arr[j]`, `j--` (shift right).
3. `arr[j + 1] = key`.

**Invariant.** Before iteration i, `arr[0..i−1]` is sorted (it contains the original first i elements in order). Inserting `key` in the right place extends the sorted prefix by one.

**Complexity = O(n + inversions).** Every shift fixes exactly one **inversion** (a pair i < j with arr[i] > arr[j]). Sorted input has 0 inversions → n − 1 comparisons, O(n). Reversed input has n(n − 1)/2 → O(n²). A "nearly sorted" array with a few out-of-place items is close to linear.

**Stable** because we stop at `arr[j] > key` (strict): an equal element is never shifted past `key`. **Online**: it can sort data as it arrives.

**Why libraries still use it.** For tiny arrays (roughly up to 16–64 elements) its low overhead and cache-friendly shifting beat O(n log n) algorithms. CPython's and Java's TimSort sort short runs with binary insertion sort, and introsort implementations (C++ `std::sort`) finish small partitions with insertion sort.

complexity.time: O(n²) worst/average, O(n) best — precisely O(n + number of inversions)

keyPoints: Sorted prefix grows by one element per iteration
Shift, do not swap: one write per moved element plus one for key
Adaptive: O(n + inversions), O(n) on sorted input
Stable and online
Used by TimSort/introsort for small ranges

visuals.title: Insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]
visuals.caption: Green range = sorted prefix, blue = key, orange = elements that were shifted right.

steps.note: Insertion sort works like sorting playing cards in your hand: the left part is always sorted, and each new card is **inserted** into its place in that part. A single element is trivially sorted.
i = 1: take `key = 2`. Everything left of it (5) is sorted; find where 2 belongs.
5 is larger than 2, so it shifts one slot right (1 shift); `key` drops into index 0.
i = 2: take `key = 4`. Everything left of it (2, 5) is sorted; find where 4 belongs.
5 is larger than 4, so it shifts one slot right (1 shift); `key` drops into index 1.
i = 3: take `key = 6`. Everything left of it (2, 4, 5) is sorted; find where 6 belongs.
`arr[2]` = 5 ≤ 6: no shifting at all — 6 stays at index 3. On sorted input every step looks like this, giving O(n).
i = 4: take `key = 1`. Everything left of it (2, 4, 5, 6) is sorted; find where 1 belongs.
2, 4, 5, 6 are larger than 1, so they shift one slot right (4 shifts); `key` drops into index 0.
i = 5: take `key = 3`. Everything left of it (1, 2, 4, 5, 6) is sorted; find where 3 belongs.
4, 5, 6 are larger than 3, so they shift one slot right (3 shifts); `key` drops into index 2.
Done: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] with 9 shifts in total. That number equals the count of **inversions** (pairs out of order) in the input, which is why insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data.

visuals.title: Shifts = inversions (measured for n = 8)
visuals.caption: Counts come from running the solution above. The work tracks how unsorted the input is, not just n.

pitfalls: Overwriting `arr[i]` before saving it in `key`
Writing `arr[j] = key` instead of `arr[j + 1] = key` after the loop
Using `>=` in the while condition, which makes it unstable and does extra shifts
Forgetting `j >= 0` and reading `arr[-1]`

followUps.question: Why is insertion sort better than bubble sort in practice?
followUps.answer: Same O(n²) bound, but it does fewer writes (one per shift instead of three per swap), stops each insertion as soon as the position is found, and is O(n + inversions). That is why libraries use it for small ranges.

followUps.question: Can binary search make it O(n log n)?
followUps.answer: Binary search cuts comparisons to O(log n) per element, but shifting elements is still O(n) per insertion, so the worst case stays O(n²) moves.

questions.title: Merge Sort
questions.prompt:
Implement **merge sort**: return the integers of `arr` sorted in ascending order by recursively sorting each half and merging the two sorted halves.

Explain the recurrence behind its running time, its memory use, and why it is stable.
constraints: Guaranteed O(n log n) time is required
hints: Two sorted arrays can be combined into one sorted array in linear time. How?
If you could sort each half, you would only need that combine step. What is the smallest array that is already sorted?
mergeSort(arr) = merge(mergeSort(left half), mergeSort(right half)); merge with two pointers, taking the smaller head each time (`<=` for stability).

approaches.name: Simple O(n²) sort
approaches.idea: Insertion/selection sort — fine for tiny inputs, too slow for 5 · 10⁴ in the worst case.

approaches.name: Top-down merge sort
approaches.idea: Recursively split in half, sort, merge with two pointers.

approaches.name: Bottom-up merge sort
approaches.idea: Iteratively merge runs of size 1, 2, 4, … — no recursion.

solution.summary: Divide the array in half, recursively sort both halves, then merge them with two pointers by repeatedly taking the smaller front element. The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n) in every case; it needs O(n) extra memory and is stable.
solution.explanation:
**Divide and conquer**
1. **Base case:** arrays of length 0 or 1 are sorted.
2. **Divide:** `mid = ⌊n/2⌋`; recursively sort `arr[0..mid)` and `arr[mid..n)`.
3. **Conquer (merge):** walk both sorted halves with pointers `i` and `j`; append the smaller of `left[i]`, `right[j]`; when one side runs out, append the rest of the other.

**Why O(n log n) — in every case.** `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn`. The recursion tree has log₂ n levels, and the merges on each level together touch all n elements, so the total is about n log₂ n. Unlike quicksort, the split is always balanced, so there is no bad input.

**Memory.** Merging needs an O(n) buffer for arrays (the recursion adds O(log n) stack). For **linked lists** merge sort needs no buffer — the merge just re-links nodes — which makes it the standard way to sort a linked list.

**Stable.** On ties (`left[i] <= right[j]`) we take from the left half first, so equal keys keep their original order. That is why stable library sorts (Java's object sort, Python's sort) are merge-based (TimSort).

**Where it shines.** Guaranteed worst case, stability, linked lists, and **external sorting** (data larger than RAM: sort chunks, then k-way merge them from disk).

complexity.time: O(n log n) best, average and worst — log n levels × O(n) merging per level
complexity.space: O(n) for the merge buffers (O(log n) recursion stack)

keyPoints: Divide in half, sort halves recursively, merge in O(n)
Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n) always
O(n) extra space for arrays; linked lists need no buffer (only the O(log n) recursion stack)
Stable thanks to `<=` in the merge
Used for linked lists, external sorting and inside TimSort

visuals.title: Recursion tree for [6, 3, 8, 5, 2, 7]
visuals.caption: Blue = call being split, orange = new sub-problems, green = merged (sorted) results, grey = consumed halves. Steps follow the real call order.

steps.note: Merge sort on [6,3,8,5,2,7]: **divide** the array in half until pieces have one element, then **merge** sorted pieces back together on the way up the recursion.
Split [6,3,8] at mid = 1 into [6] and [3,8]. [6] has one element — the base case, already sorted.
Split [3,8] at mid = 1 into [3] and [8]. [3] and [8] have one element — the base case, already sorted.
Merge the sorted halves [3] and [8] → [3,8] (2 elements, linear time).
Merge the sorted halves [6] and [3,8] → [3,6,8] (3 elements, linear time).
Split [5,2,7] at mid = 1 into [5] and [2,7]. [5] has one element — the base case, already sorted.
Split [2,7] at mid = 1 into [2] and [7]. [2] and [7] have one element — the base case, already sorted.
Merge the sorted halves [2] and [7] → [2,7] (2 elements, linear time).
Merge the sorted halves [5] and [2,7] → [2,5,7] (3 elements, linear time).
Final merge: [3,6,8] + [2,5,7] → **[2,3,5,6,7,8]**. log₂ n levels, each level merges n elements in total → O(n log n).

visuals.title: The merge step: [3, 6, 8] + [2, 5, 7]
visuals.caption: Grey = already copied to out. Each comparison emits exactly one element.

steps.note: The last merge: two **sorted** halves. Each pointer starts at the smallest unused element of its half; the smaller of the two is the next output.
Compare left[0] = 3 with right[0] = 2: take 2 from the right and advance `j`.
Compare left[0] = 3 with right[1] = 5: take 3 from the left and advance `i`.
Compare left[1] = 6 with right[1] = 5: take 5 from the right and advance `j`.
Compare left[1] = 6 with right[2] = 7: take 6 from the left and advance `i`.
Compare left[2] = 8 with right[2] = 7: take 7 from the right and advance `j`.
The right half is exhausted, so the rest of the left half (8) is copied as is — it is already sorted and larger than everything in `out`. Result: [2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] after 6 moves: O(n) per merge.

pitfalls: Using `<` in the merge — still sorted, but no longer stable
Forgetting to copy the leftover elements of one half after the main loop
Splitting with `mid = n / 2` in a way that leaves an empty half for n = 1 (infinite recursion) — the base case must be `length <= 1`
Claiming merge sort is in place for arrays

followUps.question: How do you sort a linked list in O(n log n)?
followUps.answer: Merge sort: find the middle with fast/slow pointers, cut, sort both halves recursively, and merge by re-linking nodes (like merge-two-sorted-lists). No O(n) buffer is needed.

followUps.question: How do you count inversions in an array?
followUps.answer: Augment merge sort: whenever you take `right[j]` while elements remain in the left half, all `left.length − i` remaining left elements form inversions with it. O(n log n).

followUps.question: How do you sort 100 GB of data with 1 GB of RAM?
followUps.answer: External merge sort: sort 1 GB chunks in memory and write each sorted run to disk, then k-way merge the runs with a min-heap, streaming input and output.

questions.title: Quick Sort (Lomuto partition)
questions.prompt:
Implement **quicksort** to sort an integer array in place using the **Lomuto partition** scheme.

Be ready to explain: how partition works, how you choose the pivot, what the worst case is and how to avoid it, and why quicksort is usually faster than merge sort in practice.

examples.explanation: Sorted input is the classic worst case for a fixed last-element pivot; a random pivot avoids it.

hints: Pick one element, the pivot. If every smaller element were to its left and every larger one to its right, where would the pivot be?
Partition in one pass: keep a boundary `i`; when `arr[j] <= pivot`, swap it to position `i` and move the boundary.
After partitioning, recurse on the two sides. To avoid O(n²) on sorted input, pick the pivot at random (swap it to the end first).

approaches.name: Fixed last-element pivot
approaches.idea: Lomuto with `pivot = arr[hi]`. Simple, but sorted or reverse-sorted input gives n levels of recursion.
approaches.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst (sorted input)
approaches.space: O(log n) average, O(n) worst stack

approaches.name: Randomised pivot
approaches.idea: Swap a random element to `hi` before partitioning; no fixed input is bad any more.

approaches.name: Introsort / 3-way partition
approaches.idea: Fall back to heap sort if recursion gets too deep (guaranteed O(n log n)); use 3-way (Dutch flag) partitioning for many duplicates.

solution.summary: Pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller-or-equal values go left and larger ones go right — the pivot then sits in its final position — and recurse on both sides. With a random pivot the expected time is O(n log n); a consistently bad pivot (e.g. last element on sorted input) degrades to O(n²). It sorts in place with O(log n) stack and is not stable.
solution.explanation:
**Lomuto partition (one pass)**
1. Move a randomly chosen element to `hi`; `pivot = arr[hi]`.
2. `i = lo` is the boundary: `arr[lo..i−1]` ≤ pivot, `arr[i..j−1]` > pivot.
3. For `j = lo … hi−1`: if `arr[j] <= pivot`, swap `arr[i]` and `arr[j]`, then `i++`.
4. Swap `arr[i]` with `arr[hi]`. The pivot is now at index `i`, its **final** position. Return `i`.

Then `quickSort(lo, p − 1)` and `quickSort(p + 1, hi)` — the pivot is never touched again.

**Complexity**
- **Best/average:** balanced splits → T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → **O(n log n)**.
- **Worst:** the pivot is always the min or max (fixed last pivot on sorted input, or all-equal values with Lomuto) → T(n) = T(n − 1) + O(n) → **O(n²)** and n-deep recursion.
- **Space:** in place; O(log n) stack on average. Recursing into the smaller side first and looping on the larger keeps the stack O(log n) even in bad cases.

**Choosing the pivot**
- **Random** element: no specific input can trigger the worst case; expected O(n log n).
- **Median-of-three** (first, middle, last): cheap, handles sorted input well.
- **Many duplicates:** use 3-way partitioning (`< pivot | = pivot | > pivot`) so equal keys are finished in one pass.

**Why it is fast in practice.** It is in place (no O(n) buffer), scans memory sequentially (cache-friendly), and its inner loop is tiny. Production versions combine it with insertion sort for small ranges and a heap-sort fallback (introsort, e.g. C++ `std::sort`); Java sorts primitive arrays with a **dual-pivot** quicksort.

**Not stable:** the long-distance swaps can reorder equal keys.

**Lomuto vs Hoare.** Hoare's scheme moves two pointers inward from both ends and does about 3× fewer swaps on average, but its returned index is not necessarily the pivot's final position, so the recursion is `(lo, p)` and `(p + 1, hi)`. Lomuto is easier to get right in an interview.

code.code:
import random


def quick_sort(arr, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None:
        hi = len(arr) - 1
    if lo >= hi:  # 0 or 1 element: sorted
        return arr
    p = partition(arr, lo, hi)
    quick_sort(arr, lo, p - 1)
    quick_sort(arr, p + 1, hi)
    return arr


def partition(arr, lo, hi):
    r = random.randint(lo, hi)  # random pivot, moved to the end
    arr[r], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[r]
    pivot = arr[hi]
    i = lo  # arr[lo:i] holds values <= pivot
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if arr[j] <= pivot:
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
            i += 1
    arr[i], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[i]  # pivot lands in its final place
    return i

complexity.time: O(n log n) expected with a random pivot; O(n²) worst case when the pivot is always the min/max
complexity.space: O(log n) expected recursion stack; sorting is in place

followUps.question: How do you find the k-th smallest element in O(n) average time?
followUps.answer: Quickselect: partition once, then recurse only into the side that contains index k. Expected O(n) because the work halves each time (n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n).

followUps.question: What happens with many duplicate values?
followUps.answer: With Lomuto and `<=`, all-equal input puts everything on one side → O(n²). Use a 3-way partition (Dutch national flag) or Hoare partition, which splits equal keys evenly.

followUps.question: Why does Java use dual-pivot quicksort for int[] but TimSort for objects?
followUps.answer: Primitives have no identity, so stability is irrelevant and the fastest in-place sort wins. Objects may be sorted by one field while others differ, so a stable sort (TimSort) is required by the API contract.

questions.title: Counting Sort
questions.prompt: Sort an array of integers whose values lie in a **small range** (for example exam marks 0–100 or ages 0–150) in O(n + k) time, where k is the size of the value range, using **counting sort**. Return a new sorted array and keep the sort **stable**.

examples.explanation: Offsetting by min handles negative values.

constraints: max(nums) − min(nums) ≤ 10⁶ (the range k must be small enough to allocate)
hints: If you knew how many 0s, 1s, 2s … there are, could you write the answer without comparing anything?
Count occurrences in an array indexed by value (minus the minimum).
For a stable sort, turn counts into prefix sums (end positions) and place elements walking the input from right to left.

approaches.name: Comparison sort
approaches.idea: Any general-purpose sort (merge/quick/TimSort).

approaches.name: Counting sort, simple
approaches.idea: Count each value, then write each value count[v] times in order. Fine for plain integers, but cannot carry attached data (not usable for records).

approaches.name: Counting sort, stable (prefix sums)
approaches.idea: Prefix sums give each value’s end slot; place elements right-to-left into an output array. Works for records sorted by an integer key — and is the building block of radix sort.

solution.summary: When keys are integers in a small range k, count how often each value occurs, turn the counts into prefix sums that give each value’s final positions, and place every element directly into the output — walking right to left to stay stable. O(n + k) time and space, no comparisons.
solution.explanation:
**Steps**
1. Find `min` and `max`; allocate `count` of size k = max − min + 1 (offset by `min` so negatives work).
2. **Count:** `count[x − min]++` for every x.
3. **Prefix sums:** `count[v] += count[v − 1]`. Now `count[v]` = number of elements ≤ v = one past the last index where v belongs.
4. **Place:** for i from n − 1 down to 0: `count[x − min]--`, then `out[count[x − min]] = x`.

**Why right to left?** The last occurrence of a value gets the last of its slots, the previous one the slot before, and so on, so equal keys keep their input order — the sort is **stable**. That property is exactly what **radix sort** needs when it runs counting sort once per digit.

**When to use it.** k should be O(n) or small: marks 0–100, ages, bytes 0–255, dates within a year, character frequencies. If k is huge (values up to 10⁹), the count array is impossible — use a comparison sort or radix sort instead.

**Why it beats O(n log n).** The Ω(n log n) lower bound applies only to algorithms that learn the order by comparing pairs. Counting sort uses the values as array indices instead.

code.code:
def counting_sort(nums):
    if not nums:
        return []
    lo, hi = min(nums), max(nums)
    count = [0] * (hi - lo + 1)
    for x in nums:  # 1) count each value
        count[x - lo] += 1
    for v in range(1, len(count)):  # 2) prefix sums
        count[v] += count[v - 1]
    out = [0] * len(nums)
    for x in reversed(nums):  # 3) right to left = stable
        count[x - lo] -= 1
        out[count[x - lo]] = x
    return out

complexity.time: O(n + k) — one pass to count, one over the k counts, one to place
complexity.space: O(n + k) — the output array plus the count array

Only practical when the key range k is small
Prefix sums turn counts into final positions
Right-to-left placement makes it stable
Offset by min to support negative numbers

Phase 2 — prefix sums: now `count[v]` = how many values are ≤ v, i.e. **one past the last slot** where v belongs in the output. E.g. count[3] = 7: the three 3s go into out[4..6].

i = 7: x = 3. Decrement `count[3]` to 6 and write 3 at out[6]. Walking **right to left** puts the last occurrence of each value in the last slot, which keeps equal values in their original order (stable).
i = 6: x = 0. Decrement `count[0]` to 1 and write 0 at out[1].
i = 5: x = 3. Decrement `count[3]` to 5 and write 3 at out[5].
i = 4: x = 2. Decrement `count[2]` to 3 and write 2 at out[3].
i = 3: x = 0. Decrement `count[0]` to 0 and write 0 at out[0].
i = 2: x = 3. Decrement `count[3]` to 4 and write 3 at out[4].
i = 1: x = 5. Decrement `count[5]` to 7 and write 5 at out[7].
i = 0: x = 2. Decrement `count[2]` to 2 and write 2 at out[2].
Sorted: [0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5]. Three linear passes: O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space, beating the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort bound because no two elements are ever compared.

followUps.question: How does radix sort use counting sort?
followUps.answer: LSD radix sort runs a stable counting sort on each digit (base 10 or 256), from least significant to most. Stability preserves the order from previous digits. Time O(d · (n + b)) for d digits in base b.

followUps.question: What is bucket sort and when is it O(n)?
followUps.answer: Distribute values into n buckets by range, sort each bucket (e.g. insertion sort) and concatenate. It averages O(n) when inputs are uniformly distributed, but degrades if everything lands in one bucket.

questions.title: What is a stable sort, and why does it matter?
questions.prompt: Explain what makes a sorting algorithm **stable**. Give an example where stability changes the result, name stable and unstable algorithms, and say which built-in sorts are stable in JavaScript, Python and Java.
hints: Think about records that have the same sort key but differ in other fields.
What happens to the order of those "tied" records after sorting?
Classic use: sorting by a secondary key first, then by the primary key.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "A stable sort does not crash" or "it always gives the same result." Wrong definition, no example.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Precise definition (equal keys keep their relative input order), a concrete records example, why it matters (multi-key sorts, UI tables), which algorithms are stable and why, and what the built-ins guarantee.

solution.summary: A sort is stable if elements with equal keys keep the relative order they had in the input. It only matters when records carry more than the key — e.g. sorting orders by status while keeping them in time order — and it enables multi-key sorting by repeated stable sorts. Merge sort, insertion sort, counting sort and TimSort are stable; quicksort, heap sort and selection sort are not.
solution.explanation:
**Definition.** For any two elements a and b with equal keys, if a came before b in the input, a still comes before b in the output.

**When it matters.** Only when elements have identity beyond the key: database rows, objects, UI table rows. Sorting plain integers, two equal 5s are indistinguishable, so stability is irrelevant (this is why Java sorts `int[]` with an unstable quicksort).

**Real examples**
- A bKash-style transaction list already in time order, re-sorted by status: a stable sort keeps each status group in time order.
- Spreadsheet/UI tables: click "sort by name", then "sort by department" — users expect names to stay alphabetical inside each department.
- **Radix sort** relies on a stable per-digit sort.

**Stable algorithms and why**
- **Insertion sort / bubble sort:** only move an element past strictly larger ones.
- **Merge sort:** on ties the merge takes from the left half first (`<=`).
- **Counting sort:** right-to-left placement with prefix sums.
- **TimSort:** merge-based.

**Unstable algorithms and why:** **selection sort** and **quicksort** do long-distance swaps that can jump an element over an equal one; **heap sort** reorders through the heap.

**Any sort can be made stable** by sorting `(key, originalIndex)` pairs — at the cost of extra memory.

**Built-ins**
- JavaScript: `Array.prototype.sort` must be stable since ES2019, and `toSorted` (ES2023) is stable too (V8 uses TimSort).
- Python: `list.sort()` / `sorted()` are guaranteed stable.
- Java: `Collections.sort`, `List.sort`, `Arrays.sort(Object[])` are stable (TimSort); `Arrays.sort(int[])` uses dual-pivot quicksort, which is not stable — irrelevant for primitives.

code.code:
students = [("Rafi", "B"), ("Nila", "A"), ("Tanvir", "B"), ("Sumi", "A")]
by_grade = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1])  # Python's sort is stable
print([name for name, _ in by_grade])  # ['Nila', 'Sumi', 'Rafi', 'Tanvir']

# two keys at once: a tuple key sorts by grade, then by name
by_grade_then_name = sorted(students, key=lambda s: (s[1], s[0]))

keyPoints: Stable = equal keys keep their input order
Matters for records/objects, not for plain numbers
Enables multi-key sorting by successive stable sorts
Stable: insertion, bubble, merge, counting, TimSort; unstable: selection, quick, heap
Built-ins: JS sort (ES2019+), Python sorted, Java object sorts are stable

visuals.title: Sorting students by grade: stable vs unstable
visuals.caption: Orange = grade B records, light blue = grade A records, red = ties whose order changed.

steps.note: Records in the order they were submitted. We sort **by grade only**. Rafi and Tanvir share grade B; Nila and Sumi share grade A.
**Stable sort** (merge sort, insertion sort, TimSort, JS `Array.prototype.sort`): within each grade the original order survives — Nila before Sumi, Rafi before Tanvir.

**Unstable sort** (here: selection sort, whose long-distance swaps move records past equal keys): the output is still sorted by grade, but **Tanvir now comes before Rafi**. Nothing is "wrong" with the keys — only the tie order changed.

Why it matters — **multi-key sorting**: to order by grade, then by name, first sort by name, then **stable**-sort by grade. The second sort keeps the name order inside each grade. (Or use one comparator: grade, then name.)

followUps.question: How can you make quicksort stable?
followUps.answer: Attach each element’s original index and break ties by it (sort (key, index) pairs), or partition into new arrays instead of swapping. Both cost O(n) extra memory, which removes quicksort’s main advantage.

followUps.question: Is JavaScript’s Array.prototype.sort stable?
followUps.answer: Yes. Since ES2019 the specification requires a stable sort; V8 (Chrome, Node) has used TimSort since V8 7.0.

questions.title: Which sorting algorithm would you use, and what do the built-in sorts use?
questions.prompt: Compare the common sorting algorithms (bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick, heap, counting) by time, space, stability and practical speed. **Which would you choose in which situation**, and which algorithms do the standard libraries of Python, Java and JavaScript actually use?
hints: Build a table: best / average / worst time, extra space, stable, in place.
Then think about the input: size, nearly sorted, small integer range, needs stability, memory limits, linked list, does not fit in RAM.
Finish with the libraries: TimSort (Python, Java objects, V8) and dual-pivot quicksort (Java primitives).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Quicksort is the fastest, always use it." Ignores its O(n²) worst case, stability, and that you should normally just call the library sort.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Gives the complexity table, explains the Ω(n log n) comparison bound, chooses by constraints (stability, memory, nearly sorted data, key range, external data), and knows what the built-ins use and why.

solution.summary: In real code, call the library sort: Python and Java (for objects) use TimSort — a stable, adaptive merge/insertion hybrid — V8 also uses TimSort, and Java sorts primitive arrays with dual-pivot quicksort. When choosing myself: insertion sort for tiny or nearly sorted data, merge sort when I need stability, guaranteed O(n log n) or a linked list, quicksort with a random pivot for fast in-place sorting of arrays, heap sort for an O(1)-memory worst-case guarantee, and counting/radix sort for small integer keys.
solution.explanation:
**The big picture**
- O(n²) simple sorts (bubble, selection, insertion) are only for small n — but **insertion sort** is genuinely useful for tiny or nearly sorted arrays.
- O(n log n) comparison sorts: **merge** (stable, O(n) memory), **quick** (in place, fastest on average, O(n²) worst), **heap** (in place, O(n log n) worst, not stable, cache-unfriendly so slower in practice).
- **Lower bound:** any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case — a decision tree must distinguish n! orderings, and log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n.
- Non-comparison sorts (**counting, radix**) beat that bound only for integer-like keys in a limited range.

**Which one when**
| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Normal application code | The library sort |
| n ≤ ~50 or nearly sorted | Insertion sort |
| Must be stable / sorting a linked list | Merge sort |
| Data bigger than RAM | External merge sort (sorted runs + k-way merge) |
| In place, fastest on average | Quicksort with random / median-of-three pivot |
| O(1) memory and a worst-case guarantee | Heap sort |
| Integers in a small range (marks, ages, bytes) | Counting sort (radix for wider keys) |
| Only the top k / k-th element | Heap of size k or quickselect — no full sort needed |

**What the built-ins use**
- **Python** `list.sort()` / `sorted()`: **TimSort** — finds natural runs, extends short runs with binary insertion sort, merges runs with a balanced policy (CPython 3.11+ uses the Powersort merge policy). Stable; O(n) on already sorted data; O(n log n) worst.
- **Java** `Arrays.sort(int[])` and other primitive arrays: **dual-pivot quicksort** (since Java 7) — two pivots split the range into three parts; insertion sort for tiny ranges; recent JDKs fall back to heap sort if recursion gets too deep. Not stable, but primitives have no identity.
- **Java** `Arrays.sort(Object[])`, `Collections.sort`, `List.sort`: **TimSort**, stable as the API requires.
- **JavaScript (V8, i.e. Chrome and Node.js)**: **TimSort** since V8 7.0 (2018); ES2019 requires `sort` to be stable. Without a comparator it compares values **as strings**, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`.
- **C++** `std::sort`: usually introsort (quicksort + heap sort fallback + insertion sort), not stable; `std::stable_sort` is merge-based.

**Interview tip.** Say the trade-off out loud: "I'd use the built-in sort, which is TimSort — O(n log n), stable. If I had to implement one, I'd pick merge sort for stability or quicksort with a random pivot for in-place speed."

code.code:
const nums = [10, 9, 1, 100];
console.log([...nums].sort());                // [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ]  compares as strings!
console.log([...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b)); // [ 1, 9, 10, 100 ]
console.log(nums.toSorted((a, b) => b - a));  // [ 100, 10, 9, 1 ]  ES2023, does not mutate

nums = [10, 9, 1, 100]
print(sorted(nums))        # [1, 9, 10, 100]  new list
nums.sort(reverse=True)    # in place: [100, 10, 9, 1]
words = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))  # ['Apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

Python, Java objects and V8 use TimSort (stable, adaptive); Java primitives use dual-pivot quicksort

followUps.question: Why is quicksort often faster than merge sort even though both are O(n log n)?
followUps.answer: It sorts in place (no O(n) buffer copies), scans memory sequentially (cache-friendly), and has a tight inner loop. Merge sort moves every element to a buffer and back on each level.

followUps.question: Why is TimSort so good on real data?
followUps.answer: Real data often contains already-sorted runs (appended logs, partially sorted lists). TimSort detects those runs and merges them, so it is O(n) on sorted input and much faster than O(n log n) on partially sorted input, while staying stable and O(n log n) worst case.

followUps.question: Can any comparison sort beat O(n log n)?
followUps.answer: Not in the worst case: there are n! possible orders and each comparison has two outcomes, so at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n comparisons are needed. Only non-comparison sorts (counting, radix, bucket) can do better, for restricted keys.

quiz.question: Which of these sorting algorithms is stable?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort takes from the left half on ties (`<=`), so equal keys keep their order. Quicksort and selection sort make long-distance swaps, and heap sort reorders through the heap — all three are unstable.

quiz.question: Quicksort always picks the last element as pivot. What is its running time on an already sorted array of n elements?
quiz.explanation: The pivot is always the maximum, so each partition removes only one element: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons and n-deep recursion. A random or median-of-three pivot avoids this.

quiz.question: What does this print in Node.js?

code.code: console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());

quiz.explanation: Without a comparator, `Array.prototype.sort` converts values to strings and compares them in UTF-16 order: "1" < "10" < "100" < "9". Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers.

quiz.question: With the `swapped` early-exit flag, what is bubble sort’s best-case time complexity?
quiz.explanation: On an already sorted array the first pass makes n − 1 comparisons and no swaps, so the loop breaks: O(n). Without the flag it would still do all n(n − 1)/2 comparisons.

quiz.question: Counting sort sorts n integers whose values span a range of size k. What is its time complexity?
quiz.explanation: One pass to count (n), one pass over the counts for prefix sums (k), one pass to place (n): O(n + k). It is only practical when k is not much larger than n.

quiz.question: The total number of shifts performed by insertion sort equals…
options: the number of inversions (out-of-order pairs) in the input
quiz.explanation: Each shift moves a larger element past the key, fixing exactly one inversion. So insertion sort runs in O(n + inversions): linear on nearly sorted input, quadratic on reversed input.

quiz.question: Which algorithm does Python’s `sorted()` use?
quiz.explanation: CPython uses TimSort, a stable hybrid of merge sort and binary insertion sort that exploits existing sorted runs (since 3.11 with the Powersort merge policy).

quiz.question: In Java, which algorithm does `Arrays.sort(int[])` use?
quiz.explanation: Primitive arrays use dual-pivot quicksort (since Java 7): fast and in place, and stability is meaningless for primitives. `Arrays.sort(Object[])` and `List.sort` use TimSort because objects need a stable sort.

quiz.question: At most how many swaps does selection sort perform on an array of n elements?
quiz.explanation: Each of the n − 1 rounds does at most one swap (the minimum into position i). Comparisons are always n(n − 1)/2, but swaps are at most n − 1 — its one advantage when writes are expensive.

quiz.question: How much extra memory does a standard top-down merge sort on an array need?
quiz.explanation: Merging needs a buffer as large as the range being merged: O(n) (plus O(log n) recursion stack). On a linked list, merge sort needs only O(1) extra besides the stack because merging re-links nodes.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case lower bound on the number of comparisons for any comparison-based sort?
quiz.explanation: There are n! possible orderings and each comparison has two outcomes, so a decision tree needs height ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n. Counting and radix sort escape the bound because they do not compare elements.

quiz.question: What does this print?

code.code:
pairs = [("b", 2), ("a", 1), ("c", 2), ("d", 1)]
print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1]))

quiz.explanation: The key is the number only. Python’s sort is stable, so among key 1 "a" stays before "d" and among key 2 "b" stays before "c", exactly as in the input.
